title: Advanced retrieval: hybrid ranking and reciprocal rank fusion
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects advanced retrieval: hybrid ranking and reciprocal rank fusion with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Incremental indexing needs freshness and deletion guarantees; Graph RAG represents relationships for multi-hop questions, while multimodal retrieval needs matching modalities and evidence provenance.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: Sparse retrieval such as BM25 rewards lexical evidence including rare identifiers. Dense retrieval can recover paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval combines these complementary candidate lists. Reciprocal rank fusion scores a document by summing 1/(c+rank) across ranked lists, avoiding direct comparison of incompatible raw score scales.
A cross-encoder reranker scores query-document pairs with richer joint context, usually at greater latency. Retrieve enough candidates for recall, then rerank a bounded pool for precision.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Union sparse and dense IDs, compute reciprocal rank contributions, sort with a stable tie break and retain the top candidates. Apply permission filters in both retrieval paths and again before context construction. Reranking must never reintroduce forbidden candidates.

Query rewriting, multi-query retrieval and HyDE can expand recall, but generated rewrites can change intent. Parent-child retrieval returns precise child matches plus coherent parent context. Compression should preserve evidence required for the answer rather than summarize away a negation.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: A dense query for HTTP 401 retrieves a semantically similar 403 guide but loses the exact error distinction. Conversely a lexical query for intermittent authentication fails to find a paraphrased expired-token document.

Run ablations for sparse, dense, fusion and reranking on the same queries. Inspect zero-hit, conflicting-evidence, multi-hop and tenant-isolation slices. Adding every technique without measuring its marginal value increases latency and debugging difficulty.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Incremental indexing needs freshness and deletion guarantees; Graph RAG represents relationships for multi-hop questions, while multimodal retrieval needs matching modalities and evidence provenance. These are architecture choices, not universal upgrades.

Use a retrieval-debug report showing candidate ranks at every stage. SDETs should identify whether a miss began in ingestion, candidate retrieval, fusion, reranking, context packing or generation before changing the prompt.

mistake: A dense query for HTTP 401 retrieves a semantically similar 403 guide but loses the exact error distinction. Conversely a lexical query for intermittent authentication fails to find a paraphrased expired-token document.
takeaway: Incremental indexing needs freshness and deletion guarantees; Graph RAG represents relationships for multi-hop questions, while multimodal retrieval needs matching modalities and evidence provenance.

title: Freshness, deletion and incremental indexing
objectives: Implement the worked example and validate its boundary conditions
Use the diagnostic evidence to explain a release decision
relevance: In the fictional CI quality platform, this skill connects freshness, deletion and incremental indexing with test contracts, failure triage, and evidence for release. Define and test a freshness SLO using synthetic updates and timestamps.

sections.title: Problem and intuition
paragraphs: A document store and its search index can diverge. Source deletion, permission revocation or a new version must propagate to retrieval before the service claims fresh authorized evidence. Incremental indexing updates changed records without rebuilding everything, but needs a consistent generation and deletion policy.
Freshness is a measurable lag between source change and serving visibility. A healthy database connection says nothing about whether the current index reflects required changes.

sections.title: Implement the mechanism
paragraphs: Use source version, content hash, tenant and deleted status to compute an ingestion delta. Upsert stable IDs or replace the prior chunk set atomically; mark deleted records unavailable immediately and remove their vectors. Switch serving generations only after consistency checks.

A query trace records source/index versions. Permissions are revalidated at retrieval time so stale payloads cannot authorize a revoked document. Cache invalidation includes index generation and permission scope.

sections.title: Break it and diagnose it
paragraphs: New chunks are added but old chunks are never removed, producing contradictory answers. A tombstone is cleared accidentally when a retry replays an earlier ingest event. A source permission change fails to invalidate cached context.
Test update ordering, duplicate events, out-of-order versions, deletion/reingestion and permission revocation. Reject an older source version when a newer version is already committed.

sections.title: Evaluate and apply
paragraphs: Define and test a freshness SLO using synthetic updates and timestamps. Retain old compatible indexes for rollback while ensuring revoked content is blocked across every generation.

SDETs should inspect served IDs after changes rather than trusting ingestion success logs. A release passes only when updated/deleted evidence behaves correctly through the complete retrieval and cache path.

mistake: New chunks are added but old chunks are never removed, producing contradictory answers. A tombstone is cleared accidentally when a retry replays an earlier ingest event. A source permission change fails to invalidate cached context.
takeaway: Define and test a freshness SLO using synthetic updates and timestamps.
